# Infrayard by Solvia Lab

Last substantive website update: 2026-11-05.

Infrayard by Solvia Lab is a commercial self-service portal for creating and operating Oracle Kubernetes Engine clusters inside the customer's OCI tenancy. Platform teams define templates, roles and limits. Engineers use the portal for supported cluster lifecycle workflows. No Solvia-hosted SaaS control plane is required.

Canonical website: https://www.infrayard.eu/
Company: Solvia Lab s.r.o.
Contact: hello@infrayard.eu
Support: support@infrayard.eu

## Current product scope

OKE provisioning, scale, Kubernetes upgrades, destroy and cleanup, access downloads, existing-network support, templates, resource limits, protected destroy requests, limit-increase requests, Activity and audit history, and cost estimates. Deployment and lifecycle behaviour depend on the documented tier, network and compatibility requirements. Application delivery is outside this scope. Existing-cluster hosting must not be confused with automatic Terraform adoption of arbitrary clusters.

## Deployment

Infrayard is self-hosted. It is installed with a Helm chart on a Kubernetes cluster: OKE for production, or k3s on a single VM for an evaluation; chart and images share one version number. Sign-in uses the bundled Keycloak or the customer's existing Keycloak. The chart and images come from a private container registry with a customer token; nothing is downloaded from the public website. Infrayard works under one dedicated OCI user with documented IAM policies, an API key and an Object Storage bucket for Terraform state. The portal can be limited to a VPN or company network. Setup guides: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/ and https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/.

## Commercial access

Business (one production and one test installation): EUR 3000 per month, billed monthly with a monthly commitment, or EUR 30000 annually paid upfront (EUR 2500/month equivalent). Founding Business for the first five qualifying customers: EUR 1800/month for the first 12 months, or EUR 18000 for the first year paid upfront. Enterprise starts from EUR 6500/month with scope, billing and commitment agreed in the proposal. Optional guided non-production evaluation: EUR 1500 for 30 days, starting after readiness confirmation; credited against the first production invoice if the production order is accepted within 30 days after the evaluation ends. Oracle usage is separate.

Subscriptions are arranged directly with Solvia Lab. Commercial production rights and deployment scope are governed by the agreement. Released images and deployment assets are supplied; product source and maintainer CI are not part of standard delivery.

## Customer boundary

OCI credentials, state and operational records stay in the customer's managed environment. OCI APIs, Keycloak, required OKE endpoints, image delivery and optional SMTP remain dependencies. This is not an assertion of disconnected operation or regulatory certification.

## Roadmap

AI assistance, advanced cost and policy insights, an access agent, multicloud governance, non-OCI provisioning, database options and an OCI Marketplace listing are planned work unless delivered in the customer's contracted release. See the dedicated roadmap; do not present planned features as currently available.

## Complete public documentation

## Overview

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/

Infrayard is a self-service portal for Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE). Engineers create, scale, upgrade and delete OKE clusters through a web portal. Platform administrators decide which templates, sizes and Kubernetes versions are allowed, and approve protected operations. Behind the portal, Terraform creates the resources in your own OCI tenancy.

You install Infrayard in your environment: on an OKE cluster, or on k3s on a single VM for an evaluation. Credentials, state and data stay with you.

### Find your starting point

| You want to… | Read |
| --- | --- |
| Check whether Infrayard fits your environment | [Requirements](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/requirements/) |
| Understand the components and data flow | [Architecture](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/architecture/) and [security](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/security/) |
| Install Infrayard | [Installation](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/installation/), starting with [Prepare OCI](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/) |
| Connect your company Keycloak | [Use your own Keycloak](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/) |
| Keep the portal off the internet | [Private access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/) |
| Reuse your VCNs, subnets and compartments | [Networking](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/) |
| Create, access, scale or upgrade clusters | [Cluster lifecycle](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/cluster-lifecycle/) |
| Set up templates, limits and approvals | [Administration](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/administration/) |
| Upgrade, back up or restore Infrayard | [Operations](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/) |
| Fix a problem | [Troubleshooting](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/troubleshooting/) |
| Compare plans | [Subscription](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/subscription/) |

### What Infrayard does

- **Clusters:** create, scale, upgrade and destroy OKE clusters (Basic and Enhanced), with live Terraform logs.
- **Access:** one-click kubeconfig per user, without OCI CLI setup.
- **Guardrails:** templates, per-user resource limits, protected destroy requests and limit-increase requests.
- **Visibility:** Activity inbox, audit log and cost estimates before deployment.
- **Existing infrastructure:** use your own compartments, VCNs and subnets.

Application deployment and day-to-day workload operations stay in your existing tools. See the [product scope](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/requirements/#product-scope).

### How to get started

1. [Request a demo](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=demo#demo) to see a real workflow and discuss your environment.
2. Check the [requirements](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/requirements/).
3. Start a subscription or an evaluation, receive your registry access and [install](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/installation/).

The [releases and roadmap](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/releases/) page separates what is available today from planned work.


## Architecture

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/architecture/

Infrayard runs in an environment you control: an OKE cluster, or k3s on a single VM. There is no Solvia Lab cloud service in between. Infrayard works in your OCI tenancy with its own OCI user and keeps its data in your database and your Object Storage bucket.

### Components

| Component | What it does | Runs as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Portal | Web interface: clusters, requests, access downloads, administration | `infrayard-frontend` (nginx) |
| API | Checks tokens and requests, stores data, starts and tracks Terraform jobs | `infrayard-api` |
| Terraform runner | Runs provisioning, scale, upgrade and destroy jobs | Inside `infrayard-api` |
| PostgreSQL | Clusters, jobs, users, configuration, templates, requests, audit log | `infrayard-postgresql`, or your external PostgreSQL |
| Keycloak | Sign-in, users and roles | `infrayard-keycloak`, or your existing Keycloak |
| Object Storage bucket | Terraform state of every managed cluster | In your OCI tenancy |
| OCI and OKE | The cloud resources themselves | Your OCI tenancy |

The Helm chart installs these services. An ingress controller in your cluster, such as Traefik, terminates HTTPS in front of the portal.

The portal and the bundled Keycloak share one address: the portal at `https://infrayard.example.com`, Keycloak at `https://infrayard.example.com/auth`. The portal forwards `/api` to the API and `/auth` to Keycloak; the Keycloak admin console is not reachable this way.

### What happens when a user creates a cluster

1. The user signs in through Keycloak and receives a token.
2. The portal shows the templates, options and limits that apply to this user.
3. The API checks the request: limits, template, compatibility of version, shape and image, and network settings.
4. The API starts a Terraform job with the Infrayard OCI user. Terraform stores the cluster's state in the bucket.
5. The portal streams the Terraform log. When the job ends, the cluster status, Activity entry and audit record are updated.
6. For a running cluster, the API creates a per-user ServiceAccount in the cluster and issues the kubeconfig.

Destroy requests and requests for higher limits go through the administrator review. Other operations run immediately within the user's limits.

### State and ownership

PostgreSQL holds the platform data; the bucket holds the Terraform state. Back up both and keep them consistent; see [operations](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/).

Resources created by Infrayard are managed by their cluster's Terraform state, and manual changes are overwritten by the next run. Existing networks you supply are only referenced; see [networking](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/#who-owns-what).

### Connections

| From | To | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Users | Portal (443) | Use Infrayard and sign in |
| API | OCI APIs and Object Storage (443) | Create and inspect resources, Terraform state |
| API | Kubernetes API of managed clusters (6443) | Issue kubeconfigs |
| API | Keycloak | Fetch the realm's signing keys |
| Host | Image registry (443) | Pull the Infrayard images |
| API, optional | SMTP server | E-mail notifications |

The installation needs no inbound connection from the internet when users come through a VPN. See [private access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/).

### Operating responsibility

You operate the installation, its database, secrets, storage and network, and the workloads on your clusters. Oracle provides OCI and OKE. Solvia Lab provides the Infrayard releases, documentation and the support defined in your agreement.


## Requirements and compatibility

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/requirements/

Use this page to check whether Infrayard fits your environment before you install it.

### Deployment options

| | Existing OKE cluster | Other Kubernetes (k3s, …) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intended use | Production | Evaluation on a single VM, or production |
| Tooling | `kubectl`, Helm 3.8+ | `kubectl`, Helm 3.8+ |
| Ingress | An ingress controller you install, e.g. Traefik with an OCI load balancer | Your ingress controller; k3s ships Traefik |
| TLS | cert-manager or your own certificate | cert-manager or your own certificate |
| Storage | 50 GB block volume, `oci-bv` (the OCI minimum; the chart requests 10 GiB) | 10 GiB volume from your StorageClass |
| Capacity | About 1 CPU and 2 GiB free (requests 0.9 CPU and 1.6 GiB, limits 3.7 CPU and 3.2 GiB) | Same; a k3s VM: 2 OCPUs and 8 GB memory |
| Keycloak | Bundled or your own | Bundled or your own |

At rest Infrayard uses about 0.9 GB memory and almost no CPU; Keycloak takes most of it. On a k3s VM, k3s with Traefik and cert-manager adds about 1.8 GB. Terraform jobs run inside the API, whose limit is 1 GiB.

Infrayard is tested on OKE 1.36 and k3s 1.36, both with Traefik and cert-manager. The images are built for x86 (`amd64`) and Arm (`arm64`).

### OCI

- A tenancy and a region where you create OKE clusters.
- An **anchor compartment** under which Infrayard creates clusters. See [choosing the anchor](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/#choosing-the-anchor-compartment).
- An OCI user with the [Infrayard policies](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/#3-add-the-policies), an API key and a customer secret key.
- An Object Storage bucket for Terraform state, one per Infrayard installation.
- Service limits and quotas for the clusters you plan: OKE clusters, compute cores of the worker shapes, VCNs and load balancers.

### Network

| Direction | From → to | Port |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inbound | Users → portal | 443, and 80 for redirects and Let's Encrypt |
| Outbound | Infrayard → OCI APIs and Object Storage (`*.oraclecloud.com`) | 443 |
| Outbound | Infrayard → image registry | 443 |
| Outbound | Infrayard → Terraform providers: `registry.terraform.io`, `releases.hashicorp.com`, GitHub releases | 443 |
| Outbound | Infrayard → Kubernetes API of each managed cluster | 6443 |
| Outbound | Users → Kubernetes API of their clusters, for `kubectl` | 6443 |
| Outbound, optional | Infrayard → your SMTP server | 587 or your port |
| Outbound, optional | Infrayard → your own Keycloak | 443 |

The portal needs no inbound connection from the internet if users come through a VPN; see [private access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/).

### Identity

Sign-in uses Keycloak: either the Keycloak bundled with Infrayard (realm, client and admin role are created automatically) or a realm in your existing Keycloak 22 or newer. See [Use your own Keycloak](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/).

### Costs outside the subscription

The subscription covers the Infrayard software. Your Oracle Cloud bill covers the OKE clusters and their nodes, load balancers and storage, and the host that runs Infrayard: capacity and one block volume in your cluster (50 GB on OKE, the OCI minimum) plus a load balancer for the ingress, or the VM for k3s.

### OKE versions, shapes and images

Which Kubernetes versions, shapes and node images exist depends on your region and tenancy. Administrators sync them from OCI in **Admin → Configuration** and enable what users may choose. Newly synced Kubernetes versions stay disabled until an administrator enables them.

The deploy and template forms only offer Kubernetes versions that have a node image for the selected shape. If Infrayard cannot check this with OCI, deployment is blocked rather than allowing an unverified combination. See [troubleshooting](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/troubleshooting/#missing-versions-or-shapes).

### Basic and Enhanced clusters

The platform can allow Basic, Enhanced or both OKE cluster types. These are Oracle service tiers, separate from Infrayard subscription plans.

| Operation | Basic | Enhanced |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add or remove nodes and pools | Automatic | Automatic |
| Change a pool's shape, OCPUs, memory or storage | Needs rolling worker cycling | Automatic rollout |
| Kubernetes upgrade | Control plane first, then a rolling worker refresh | Automatic control plane and worker rollout |
| OCI control-plane charges | Oracle's Basic pricing | Oracle's Enhanced pricing |

See [cluster lifecycle](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/cluster-lifecycle/#cluster-tiers) for the steps.

### Product scope

Infrayard provisions and manages OKE clusters: create, access, scale, upgrade and destroy, with templates, limits, requests, cost estimates, audit records and existing-network support.

- Deploying applications, CI/CD and application databases stay in your existing tools.
- Running Infrayard **on** an existing OKE cluster is different from **managing** that cluster with Infrayard. Infrayard manages only clusters it created; existing clusters are not imported.
- One installation manages one anchor compartment tree. Unrelated trees need the tenancy root as anchor or separate installations.
- Existing subnets need their VCN as well, and prepared routing. The public API endpoint mode needs Infrayard-managed networking.
- AI assistance, an access agent and non-OCI clouds are on the [roadmap](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/releases/#planned-work), not in the product today.
- Running in your tenancy does not by itself make the setup compliant, highly available or air-gapped.


## Security and access

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/security/

Infrayard runs entirely in your environment. OCI credentials, Terraform state, the database and logs stay with you; there is no Solvia Lab cloud service in the path, and Infrayard sends no data to Solvia Lab.

### Identity and roles

Sign-in uses OpenID Connect with the Authorization Code flow and PKCE, handled by Keycloak: the one bundled with Infrayard or a realm in your existing Keycloak. The portal is a public client, so no client secret is stored in the browser. The API checks the signature, issuer and audience of every token.

Infrayard creates a user record on the first sign-in. Access is controlled by Keycloak roles or groups:

- **Admin role**: the administration area, all clusters, users, configuration, templates, requests and audit log.
- **Access role** (optional): only users with it may sign in. Use it with a shared company realm.
- **Template roles**: a template can require a role, so only some users see it.

When a role is removed or the Keycloak session ends, the user is signed out within a few minutes. Details: [Use your own Keycloak](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/#roles).

### OCI credentials

Infrayard acts in OCI as one service user with an API key. Its policies are scoped to the anchor compartment; read access covers the tenancy so that regions, shapes and networks can be listed. See [Prepare OCI](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/#3-add-the-policies).

Where the credentials are stored:

| Secret | Where |
| --- | --- |
| OCI API private key | Secret `infrayard-oci-key`, mounted read-only into the API |
| S3 key for the state bucket, database and Keycloak passwords | Secrets created by the chart from your values |

Keep these in your secret manager. Never send them in support requests.

Rotating the API key: add a new key to the OCI user, update the secret and the fingerprint, roll out, then delete the old key in OCI.

### Kubernetes access

Users download a kubeconfig from a running cluster's detail page. It works with plain `kubectl`, without the OCI CLI:

```bash
export KUBECONFIG=~/Downloads/oke-my-cluster-kubeconfig.yaml
kubectl get nodes
```

How it works:

- Each Infrayard user gets their own ServiceAccount in the namespace `infrayard-system` of the cluster, so Kubernetes audit logs show the actual person.
- The ServiceAccount is bound to **`cluster-admin`**. Everyone who may download a kubeconfig for a cluster has full rights on it.
- The embedded token is valid for up to 30 days; the cluster may shorten that. Download a new kubeconfig when it expires.
- To revoke a user's access to a cluster at once, delete their ServiceAccount: `kubectl delete serviceaccount <user> -n infrayard-system`.

Users with an OCI CLI setup can download an alternative kubeconfig that authenticates through the OCI CLI.

Cluster owners download access for their clusters; administrators can download it for every cluster in **All Clusters → Details**. Include this in your access review.

The kubeconfig does not create a network path. Users need a route to the cluster's API endpoint; see [networking](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/#kubernetes-api-endpoint-access).

### SSH access

Terraform generates an SSH key pair for each cluster's worker nodes. The private key is stored in the Infrayard database and can be downloaded from the cluster's detail page. Treat it as a credential, and treat database backups as sensitive for this reason.

### Audit and approvals

Every lifecycle operation records who did what, on which cluster, the result and the duration. Destroy requests and limit-increase requests record the submission and the decision. Administrators can force-destroy a cluster for incident response; this is recorded too.

The Activity inbox shows lifecycle events, request outcomes and limit changes. Optional e-mail notifications send event details to the configured recipients through your SMTP server.

### Network exposure

The portal is the only inbound endpoint. The Keycloak admin console is not exposed: it is reached with `kubectl port-forward`. We recommend making the portal reachable [only from your VPN](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/).

Outbound, Infrayard needs OCI APIs, the image registry and the cluster APIs; see [requirements](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/requirements/#network).

### Hardening built in

- The Infrayard, Keycloak and PostgreSQL containers run as non-root users and drop all Linux capabilities; the API and the portal also use read-only root file systems.
- The portal sends security headers (`X-Content-Type-Options`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy`) and redirects HTTP to HTTPS.
- Configuration or secret changes roll the affected pods automatically on `helm upgrade`.

### Your security review

Before production, review TLS and exposure, OCI policy scope, who holds the admin role, kubeconfig rights, secret storage, database and state backups, and log access. Security questionnaires and additional evidence can be arranged through [Enterprise](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=enterprise#demo).


## Networking and existing infrastructure

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/

Each cluster needs a network, and its Kubernetes API must be reachable from Infrayard and from your users. This page explains what Infrayard creates by default, how to reuse your own VCNs, subnets and compartments, and which access mode to choose for the Kubernetes API.

### Default setup

Without any overrides, Infrayard creates a complete network for every cluster, in the cluster's own compartment:

- A **VCN** whose /16 range is derived from the cluster's /24 CIDR.
- A **private worker subnet** (/24). Worker nodes have no public IPs.
- A **public load balancer subnet** for Kubernetes `LoadBalancer` services.
- A **public API endpoint subnet**, only in the restricted public API mode (below).
- Internet, NAT and service gateways with route tables.
- Security lists with the rules OKE needs, plus the TCP/6443 allowlist for the API.

All of it belongs to the cluster's Terraform state and is removed when the cluster is destroyed.

### Kubernetes API endpoint access

Choose the mode in **Admin → Configuration → OCI Settings → Kubernetes API Access**: the box **Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist** and the list **Allowed API CIDRs**. The setting applies to clusters created afterwards.

| Mode | Where the API is | Who can reach it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Private endpoint (box off, default) | Private subnet, no public IP | Anything with a route into the VCN: VPN through a DRG, FastConnect, a bastion, or Infrayard running in a peered network |
| Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist | Dedicated public subnet | Only the CIDR ranges you list; `0.0.0.0/0` is rejected |

With **Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist** on, list both in **Allowed API CIDRs**:

- your **VPN or office egress** ranges, so users can run `kubectl`, and
- the **outbound address of Infrayard** itself (NAT gateway or VM public IP), because Infrayard calls the cluster API to issue kubeconfigs.

This mode avoids routing every cluster VCN to your network, which helps when DRG attachments are costly or local peering limits are reached. Users still connect from the VPN or office network.

The kubeconfig only provides authentication. Without a network path to port 6443, `kubectl` times out.

### Bringing your own network

In the deploy form, the **Advanced** tab accepts existing OCIDs. Infrayard then skips creating those resources:

| Field | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Existing Compartment OCID | Resources go into this compartment instead of a new one |
| Existing VCN OCID | Uses your VCN; Infrayard creates only the cluster subnets and their security lists inside it |
| Existing Subnet OCID | Worker nodes go into your subnet; requires the VCN OCID as well |

Supported combinations:

| You provide | Infrayard creates and manages |
| --- | --- |
| Nothing | Compartment, VCN, subnets, gateways, route tables, security lists, cluster |
| Compartment | VCN and the complete network inside that compartment, cluster |
| VCN (optionally compartment) | Subnets and security lists in your VCN, cluster. Your gateways and route tables are used as they are |
| VCN and subnet (optionally compartment) | Only the cluster and node pools. Your network is used read-only |
| Subnet without VCN | Rejected before Terraform starts |

Rules:

- **Stay inside the anchor.** A supplied compartment must be the anchor compartment or any compartment below it. Others are rejected before Terraform starts, because the OCI policies only cover the anchor subtree.
- **No automatic discovery.** Supplying only a compartment does not reuse a VCN that already exists in it; Infrayard creates a new one.
- **Routing must be ready.** With your own VCN or subnet, the worker subnet needs a route `0.0.0.0/0` to a NAT gateway (or your egress path) and a route for `all-<region>-services-in-oracle-services-network` to a service gateway. Otherwise nodes cannot register.
- **Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist** needs an Infrayard-managed VCN. While this mode is on, deployments with an existing VCN or subnet are rejected; an existing compartment is fine.
- **Sharing a compartment:** to place several clusters in one compartment, create a compartment for them and supply it to each cluster. Do not reuse a compartment that Infrayard created for another cluster.

The OCID fields check the OCID type and offer autocomplete lists of the compartments, VCNs and subnets Infrayard can see.

### Choosing the anchor compartment

The anchor is set at installation and can be changed in **Admin → Configuration**. Typical choices:

| Anchor | Good for | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A dedicated compartment, e.g. `infrayard` | Clear separation and the narrowest permissions | Existing networks must be inside it |
| An existing compartment such as `platform` | Reusing networks and compartments that already exist there | The policies grant management of everything below it |
| The tenancy root | Reusing anything in the tenancy | Policies at tenancy scope; widest permissions |

One installation cannot span several unrelated compartment trees. Use the tenancy root as anchor, or run separate installations.

### Who owns what

- Resources Infrayard creates are managed by the cluster's Terraform state. Manual changes in the OCI Console are overwritten by the next scale or upgrade.
- Resources you supply (compartment, VCN, subnet) are only referenced, never changed or deleted.

### Custom security rules

The default security lists cover what OKE needs. For your own rules, for example extra node ports, restricted egress or network security groups, supply your own subnet with those rules already in place. Infrayard then creates no security list of its own.

### The Infrayard installation itself

To make the portal reachable only from your VPN, see [private access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/).


## Installation

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/installation/

Infrayard runs on a Kubernetes cluster in your environment: an OKE cluster for production, or k3s on a single VM for an evaluation. Both use the same Helm chart, images and values. Installation takes about an hour, including the OCI preparation.

### Choose your deployment path

| | Existing OKE cluster | Other Kubernetes (k3s, …) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Good for | Production | Evaluation on a single VM, or production |
| Installed with | Helm chart | Helm chart |
| Ingress and TLS | Your ingress controller (e.g. Traefik) and cert-manager | Same; k3s ships Traefik |
| Database storage | OCI Block Volume (`oci-bv`), 50 GB | Your StorageClass (k3s: `local-path`) |
| Keycloak | Bundled or your own | Bundled or your own |
| Guide | [Install on Kubernetes](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/) | [Install on Kubernetes](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/) |

**For an evaluation**, one VM with k3s is enough: install k3s with its [quick start](https://docs.k3s.io/quick-start), then follow the Kubernetes guide. We recommend 2 OCPUs and 8 GB memory. Measured on our k3s demo VM at rest, the whole VM (Oracle Linux, k3s, Traefik, cert-manager and Infrayard) uses about 3.5 GB, of which Infrayard about 0.9 GB. The images run on x86 and Arm (Ampere A1) shapes.

Both paths run one replica of each service, and Kubernetes restarts a service that fails. Neither is a high-availability setup for the portal itself. Your OKE clusters keep running if Infrayard is down.

### What you receive

When your order is accepted and the first invoice is paid, or when your evaluation starts, your technical contact receives an onboarding e-mail with:

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Registry user and token | Personal to your organisation; the token can only pull |
| Registry | `registry.gitlab.com` |
| Helm chart | `oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard` |
| Images | `registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/api` and `registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/frontend` |
| Version to install | A number such as `1.4.0`; chart and images share it |
| Support | [support@infrayard.eu](mailto:support@infrayard.eu) |

The guides on this site are written so that your team can install Infrayard with these values on its own. Nothing is downloaded from a public website: the chart and the images come only from this registry.

The token reads the registry and nothing else, for the term of your subscription or evaluation. Store it in your secret manager and ask [support](mailto:support@infrayard.eu) for a new one if it leaks.

### From the e-mail to the first cluster

1. **[Prepare OCI](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/)**, about 20 minutes: the service user, policies, API key, state bucket and S3 key. Needed for every path.
2. **Prepare the host:** an OKE cluster you already run, or a VM with k3s from the [k3s quick start](https://docs.k3s.io/quick-start).
3. **[Install with Helm](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/)**, about 30 minutes, including DNS and the certificate.
4. **Configure and test:** sign in, set up **Admin → Configuration** and create a test cluster, as in [step 7 of the guide](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/#7-sign-in). The test cluster proves the OCI policies, the state bucket and the network path to the cluster API.
5. **Give people access:** [add users](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/#add-users) in the bundled Keycloak, or connect [your own Keycloak](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/).
6. **Recommended:** make the portal reachable [only from your VPN](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/).
7. **Before production use:** schedule the daily [database backup](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/#backups) and read how to [upgrade](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/#upgrade-infrayard).

If a step fails, look it up in [troubleshooting](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/troubleshooting/#installation). If that does not help, write to [support](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/troubleshooting/#contact-support) with the details listed there.

### What you prepare

| Item | Example |
| --- | --- |
| OCI tenancy, region and anchor compartment | `eu-frankfurt-1`, compartment `infrayard` |
| OCI service user with policies, API key and S3 key | See [Prepare OCI](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/) |
| A DNS name for the portal | `infrayard.example.com` |
| A way to get a TLS certificate | Let's Encrypt (automatic) or your company CA |
| A host | A Kubernetes cluster with about 1 CPU and 2 GiB free, or a VM with 2 OCPUs and 8 GB memory for k3s |
| Network paths | Users → portal (443); Infrayard → OCI APIs, registry, cluster APIs (6443) |

Details for each item are in [requirements](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/requirements/).


## Prepare OCI

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/

Infrayard creates OKE clusters with Terraform under one OCI user. This page creates that user, its permissions, an API key, the Terraform state bucket and the S3 key for the bucket. Every installation path needs these steps. Plan about 20 minutes in the OCI Console, or use the [OCI CLI variant](#the-same-steps-with-the-oci-cli) below.

You need a user with administrator rights in the tenancy for these steps; Infrayard itself never gets them.

At the end you have the values from the [checklist](#values-checklist).

### 1. Choose the anchor compartment

Infrayard creates everything it manages **under one compartment**, the anchor. By default each cluster gets its own child compartment with its network and node pools; a cluster can also use an existing compartment inside the anchor.

- Create a dedicated compartment, for example `infrayard`, or choose an existing one.
- Note its **OCID** (Identity & Security → Compartments → your compartment).
- Note its **name path**, which the policies use. For a nested compartment, write it with colons, for example `platform:infrayard`.

Administrators can switch the anchor and region later in **Admin → Configuration**. The OCI user can only manage what the policies below allow.

### 2. Create the user and group

In **Identity & Security → Domains → Default domain**:

1. **Groups → Create group**, name `InfrayardServiceGroup`.
2. **Users → Create user**: first name `Infrayard`, last name `Service`, username `infrayard-svc`. An e-mail address is required; use a team mailbox. Clear **Use the email address as the username**.
3. Open the user, **Groups → Assign user to groups**, select `InfrayardServiceGroup`.
4. Copy the **user OCID** from the user's page.

The user does not need a console password.

### 3. Add the policies

**Identity & Security → Policies**, select the **root compartment**, then **Create policy**. Name it `infrayard-service`, open the **manual editor** and paste the statements. Replace `infrayard` with your compartment name path.

```text
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage cluster-family in compartment infrayard
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage virtual-network-family in compartment infrayard
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage instance-family in compartment infrayard
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage compartments in compartment infrayard
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to manage object-family in compartment infrayard
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to read all-resources in tenancy
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to read tenancies in tenancy
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to inspect compartments in tenancy
Allow group InfrayardServiceGroup to use tag-namespaces in tenancy
Allow service OKE to manage all-resources in tenancy
```

What each part is for:

| Statements | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `cluster-family`, `virtual-network-family`, `instance-family` | Create, scale, upgrade and delete OKE clusters, their VCNs and worker nodes |
| `compartments` | Create one child compartment per cluster and remove it on destroy |
| `object-family` | Read and write Terraform state in the bucket from step 5 |
| `read all-resources`, `read tenancies`, `inspect compartments` | List regions, shapes, Kubernetes versions, images and existing networks |
| `use tag-namespaces` | Required when your tenancy applies tag defaults to new resources. Infrayard itself sets free-form tags |
| `Allow service OKE …` | Lets the OKE service itself work in the tenancy. Keep it in this policy even if another policy already has it; a duplicate statement does no harm |

If the group lives in a domain other than **Default**, write it as `group 'MyDomain'/'InfrayardServiceGroup'`.

Keep [existing VCNs and subnets](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/#bringing-your-own-network) that clusters should use inside the anchor compartment; the policies above then cover them.

### 4. Create the API key

1. Open the `infrayard-svc` user → **API keys → Add API key**.
2. Select **Generate API key pair**, click **Download private key** and save it as `oci_api_key.pem`.
3. Click **Add**. The configuration preview shows `user`, `fingerprint`, `tenancy` and `region`. Note all four.

The private key is the most sensitive item of the installation. Store it in your secret manager and do not e-mail it.

### 5. Create the Terraform state bucket

1. **Storage → Object Storage → Buckets**, select the **anchor compartment**, then **Create bucket**.
2. Name: `infrayard-tfstate`. Keep the default **Standard** tier and enable **Object versioning**. Versioning keeps earlier state versions if something goes wrong.
3. Note the **namespace** shown on the bucket page (also: `oci os ns get`).

Use a separate bucket for every Infrayard installation, for example for a test and a production portal. Infrayard stores each cluster's state as `<user name>/<cluster name>.tfstate`, so two installations that share a bucket can overwrite each other's state.

Use the same region as the one in the API key preview.

### 6. Create the S3 key for the bucket

Terraform reaches the bucket through the S3-compatible API, which needs its own key.

1. Open the `infrayard-svc` user → **Customer secret keys → Generate secret key**, name `infrayard-tfstate`.
2. Copy the **secret key** right away. OCI shows it only once.
3. Copy the **access key** from the list.

### The same steps with the OCI CLI

Instead of the Console you can run steps 1–6 with the OCI CLI, signed in as a tenancy administrator. The commands were tested in this order; they keep the generated values in shell variables and write the key files to the current directory. Run them in an empty directory that only you can read (`mkdir -m 700 infrayard-oci && cd infrayard-oci`).

```bash
# Your tenancy OCID, as in ~/.oci/config of the administrator
T=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa…

# 1. Anchor compartment (skip and set C=<ocid> to use an existing one)
C=$(oci iam compartment create -c $T --name infrayard \
      --description "Infrayard anchor compartment" \
      --wait-for-state ACTIVE --query data.id --raw-output)

# 2. Group and user, user in the group
G=$(oci iam group create -c $T --name InfrayardServiceGroup \
      --description "Infrayard service user" --query data.id --raw-output)
U=$(oci iam user create -c $T --name infrayard-svc \
      --description "Infrayard service user" --email platform-team@example.com \
      --query data.id --raw-output)
oci iam group add-user --group-id $G --user-id $U

# 3. Policy: save the ten statements from step 3 as a JSON list in policy.json,
#    one string per statement: ["Allow group …", "Allow group …", …]
oci iam policy create -c $T --name infrayard-service \
  --description "Infrayard service user" --statements file://policy.json

# 4. API key: generate it locally and upload the public part
umask 077
openssl genrsa -out oci_api_key.pem 2048
openssl rsa -pubout -in oci_api_key.pem -out oci_api_key_public.pem
FP=$(oci iam user api-key upload --user-id $U \
       --key-file oci_api_key_public.pem --query data.fingerprint --raw-output)

# 5. State bucket with versioning, and the namespace
oci os bucket create -c $C --name infrayard-tfstate --versioning Enabled
NS=$(oci os ns get --query data --raw-output)

# 6. S3 key: "id" is the access key, "key" the secret key (shown only once)
oci iam customer-secret-key create --user-id $U --display-name infrayard-tfstate \
  --query 'data.{access_key:id,secret_key:key}' --output json > s3-key.json

echo "tenancy=$T user=$U fingerprint=$FP compartment=$C namespace=$NS"
```

The last line prints the values for the [checklist](#values-checklist); the S3 key pair is in `s3-key.json`. Store `oci_api_key.pem` and `s3-key.json` in your secret manager and delete the local copies after the installation.

### Check the setup

A new user and API key take **a few minutes** to work in every OCI service. During that time some calls fail with `401 NotAuthenticated` even though everything is set up correctly; in our tests Identity accepted the key first, Container Engine and Object Storage about two minutes later. Wait five minutes before you start the installation or before you look for a mistake.

To check the new user from your workstation, write a CLI configuration file for it (values from the [checklist](#values-checklist)):

```ini
# infrayard-oci-config
[DEFAULT]
user=ocid1.user.oc1..aaaa…
fingerprint=12:34:56:…
tenancy=ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa…
region=eu-frankfurt-1
key_file=/full/path/to/oci_api_key.pem
```

These three commands must succeed. They print the compartment name, a list of Kubernetes versions, and an empty list for the new bucket:

```bash
oci --config-file infrayard-oci-config iam compartment get \
  --compartment-id <anchor-compartment-ocid> --query data.name --raw-output
oci --config-file infrayard-oci-config ce cluster-options get \
  --cluster-option-id all --query 'data."kubernetes-versions"'
oci --config-file infrayard-oci-config os object list --bucket-name infrayard-tfstate
```

`NotAuthorizedOrNotFound` (404) instead means a policy is missing or names the wrong group or compartment. Infrayard runs the same kind of calls when an administrator syncs shapes and versions in **Admin → Configuration**.

### Values checklist

| Value | Example | Where it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tenancy OCID | `ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa…` | API key preview |
| User OCID | `ocid1.user.oc1..aaaa…` | Step 2 |
| Fingerprint | `12:34:56:…` | API key preview |
| Region | `eu-frankfurt-1` | API key preview |
| Private key file | `oci_api_key.pem` | Step 4 |
| Anchor compartment OCID | `ocid1.compartment.oc1..aaaa…` | Step 1 |
| Object Storage namespace | `frxyz1abcd` | Step 5 |
| State bucket | `infrayard-tfstate` | Step 5 |
| S3 access key and secret key | `0a1b2c…` | Step 6 |

Continue with [Install on Kubernetes](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/).


## Install on Kubernetes

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/

This guide installs Infrayard with Helm into a Kubernetes cluster you already run: an OKE cluster, k3s or another distribution. The steps are the same everywhere; where OKE and k3s differ, both variants are shown. Infrayard is tested with this guide on OKE (Kubernetes 1.36, one `VM.Standard.E4.Flex` worker with 1 OCPU and 8 GB) and on k3s, both with Traefik and cert-manager.

Time needed: about 30 minutes, after [Prepare OCI](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/).

### What you need

- A Kubernetes cluster and `kubectl` access. Step 1 installs cluster-wide resources (cert-manager and its CRDs, the Let's Encrypt issuer) and needs cluster-admin rights; the Infrayard chart itself creates only namespaced resources.
- [Helm](https://helm.sh/docs/intro/install/) 3.8 or newer on your workstation.
- An ingress controller. OKE has none by default; k3s ships Traefik.
- [cert-manager](https://cert-manager.io/) for Let's Encrypt certificates, or your own TLS certificate.
- A StorageClass for the PostgreSQL volume. The chart requests 10 GiB. OKE: `oci-bv`, which creates a 50 GB block volume, the OCI minimum. k3s: `local-path`.
- Free capacity of about 1 CPU and 2 GiB memory. Limits allow peaks up to 3.7 CPU and 3.2 GiB.
- Outbound internet access from the pods. Each cluster deployment downloads the Terraform providers from `registry.terraform.io`, `releases.hashicorp.com` and GitHub releases. On OKE with private worker nodes, this traffic goes through the VCN's NAT gateway; a service gateway alone is not enough.
- A DNS name for the portal, for example `infrayard.example.com`. Keycloak is served on the same name under `/auth`, so one name is enough.
- The values from the [OCI checklist](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/#values-checklist).
- Your registry access from the onboarding e-mail: user, token, registry address and the Infrayard version (for example `1.4.0`; use it wherever `<version>` appears below).

The examples use the namespace `infrayard`, the release name `infrayard` and the registry `registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard`. Use the registry address and version from your onboarding e-mail.

### 1. Ingress controller and certificates

Skip this step if your cluster already has an ingress controller and cert-manager.

**OKE: install Traefik.** It creates an OCI flexible load balancer with a public IP:

```bash
helm repo add traefik https://traefik.github.io/charts
helm install traefik traefik/traefik -n traefik --create-namespace \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape"=flexible \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-min"=10 \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-max"=100
```

Use `--set-string`: annotations must be strings, and with `--set` Helm reads `10` and `100` as numbers and the install fails. The load balancer gets its public IP within about a minute; `kubectl get svc -n traefik traefik` shows it as `EXTERNAL-IP`.

The load balancer subnet must allow TCP 80 and 443 from the internet in its security list or network security group: 80 for Let's Encrypt, 443 for users. Clusters created by Infrayard have these rules. OKE opens the node ports from the load balancer to the worker nodes on its own.

For a portal reachable only from your VPN, use an internal load balancer instead; see [private access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/).

**k3s:** Traefik is already running in `kube-system`.

**cert-manager** (both):

```bash
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io
helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager -n cert-manager --create-namespace \
  --set crds.enabled=true
```

Then create a Let's Encrypt issuer. It needs no e-mail address; Let's Encrypt no longer sends expiry e-mails, and cert-manager renews the certificate on its own:

```bash
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: traefik
EOF
```

Let's Encrypt must reach the portal on port 80 from the internet. If it cannot, use your own certificate (step 4).

### 2. Log in to the registry

The chart and the images are in the same private registry. Log in once with the token from your onboarding e-mail:

```bash
helm registry login registry.gitlab.com -u <registry-user>
# Password: your registry token
```

In scripts, pass the token on standard input instead: `printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | helm registry login registry.gitlab.com -u <registry-user> --password-stdin`.

Check that you can read the chart:

```bash
helm show chart oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard --version <version>
```

The output starts with `Pulled: …` and ends with `name: infrayard` and `version: <version>`. An error with `401`, `403` or `denied` means the login is missing or the token cannot read the registry; see [troubleshooting](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/troubleshooting/#installation).

### 3. Create the namespace and secrets

Two secrets are created by hand so that they never appear in Helm values. Run the commands from a directory that contains `oci_api_key.pem`:

```bash
kubectl create namespace infrayard

# Lets Kubernetes pull the images
kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred -n infrayard \
  --docker-server=registry.gitlab.com \
  --docker-username=<registry-user> \
  --docker-password=<registry-token>

# OCI API private key of the infrayard-svc user
kubectl create secret generic infrayard-oci-key -n infrayard \
  --from-file=oci_api_key.pem=./oci_api_key.pem
```

The key name inside the secret must be `oci_api_key.pem`. Without this secret the API pod stays in `Init` or `ContainerCreating`.

### 4. Write the values files

Keep settings and passwords in two files. `values.yaml` can go into your configuration repository; `secrets.yaml` belongs in your secret manager.

`values.yaml`:

```yaml
global:
  domain: infrayard.example.com
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: regcred

api:
  image:
    repository: registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/api
  oci:
    tenancyOcid: ocid1.tenancy.oc1..aaaa...
    userOcid: ocid1.user.oc1..aaaa...
    fingerprint: "12:34:56:78:90:ab:cd:ef:12:34:56:78:90:ab:cd:ef"
    region: eu-frankfurt-1
    namespace: frxyz1abcd
    parentCompartmentOcid: ocid1.compartment.oc1..aaaa...
  terraform:
    stateBucket: infrayard-tfstate

frontend:
  image:
    repository: registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/frontend

postgresql:
  storage:
    storageClass: oci-bv        # OKE. k3s: local-path. Empty: cluster default

keycloak:
  realmImport:
    initialAdmin:               # first Infrayard administrator
      username: admin
      email: admin@example.com

ingress:
  className: traefik            # or nginx, or your controller's class
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt
  tls:
    enabled: true
    secretName: infrayard-tls
```

`secrets.yaml`. Generate each of the three passwords with `openssl rand -hex 24`; hex passwords contain no characters that need escaping:

```yaml
postgresql:
  auth:
    password: "<database password>"
keycloak:
  admin:
    password: "<Keycloak master admin password>"
  realmImport:
    initialAdmin:
      password: "<temporary password of the first admin>"
api:
  terraform:
    s3AccessKey: "<S3 access key>"
    s3SecretKey: "<S3 secret key>"
```

```bash
chmod 600 secrets.yaml
```

Notes:

- **Own certificate instead of Let's Encrypt:** create the secret with `kubectl create secret tls infrayard-tls -n infrayard --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem` and remove the `cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer` annotation.
- **ingress-nginx:** set `className: nginx` and add the annotations `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"` and `nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"`, so that live Terraform logs are not cut off.
- **Your own Keycloak** instead of the bundled one: see [Use your own Keycloak](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/) before installing.
- **E-mail notifications** (optional): set `api.email.enabled: true`, `api.email.adminEmails` and the `api.email.smtp` block, with the SMTP password in `secrets.yaml`.
- **Test or demo installation:** `frontend.robots.noindex: true` asks search engines not to index the portal.
- **Single-node clusters:** the chart tolerates the control-plane taint by default, so all pods can run on one k3s node.

### 5. Install

```bash
helm install infrayard oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard \
  --version <version> -n infrayard -f values.yaml -f secrets.yaml
```

The chart version selects the matching image version automatically; do not set an image tag.

Watch the pods until all four are `Running` and ready, usually within two minutes. Keycloak is the last one, because it imports the realm on the first start:

```bash
kubectl get pods -n infrayard -w
```

```text
NAME                                  READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
infrayard-api-6c9f7d8b5-x2kqp         1/1     Running   0          2m
infrayard-frontend-5bd8c7f9d4-7wq9z   1/1     Running   0          2m
infrayard-keycloak-7d9b6f5c8-k4m2n    1/1     Running   0          2m
infrayard-postgresql-0                1/1     Running   0          2m
```

### 6. Point DNS to the cluster

Find the external IP of the ingress controller:

```bash
kubectl get svc -n traefik traefik        # OKE with Traefik from step 1
kubectl get svc -n kube-system traefik    # k3s
```

Create an `A` record from `infrayard.example.com` to the `EXTERNAL-IP`.

**k3s on a cloud VM** (for example OCI Compute): k3s publishes Traefik on the node's own address, so `EXTERNAL-IP` shows the VM's **private** IP, such as `10.0.0.12`. Point DNS to the VM's **public** IP instead, and allow TCP 80 and 443 in the VM's security list or network security group and in the host firewall. For a VPN-only portal, use the private IP; see [private access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/).

Once DNS resolves, cert-manager obtains the certificate, usually within two minutes:

```bash
kubectl get certificate -n infrayard
# NAME            READY   SECRET          AGE
# infrayard-tls   True    infrayard-tls   2m
```

### 7. Sign in

Open `https://infrayard.example.com` and sign in with the first admin's user name and temporary password. Keycloak asks for a new password right away.

Then, in **Admin → Configuration**:

1. Check the region and the anchor compartment.
2. **Sync** shapes and Kubernetes versions from OCI and enable the ones your users may choose. New versions start disabled.
3. Set **Kubernetes API Access** under **OCI Settings**. Infrayard calls the API of every new cluster on port 6443 to issue kubeconfigs, so it needs a network path to it. With the box off (the default), clusters get a private endpoint. Infrayard creates a new VCN for each cluster unless you supply one, so it reaches a private endpoint only if its own network is routed into that VCN; without such a route the cluster still deploys, but the kubeconfig download fails. To use a public endpoint instead, turn on **Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist**, enter your VPN or office ranges and Infrayard's own outbound address in **Allowed API CIDRs**, and click **Save OCI settings**. On OKE with private worker nodes, that address is the public IP of the NAT gateway in the VCN of the cluster that runs Infrayard:

   ```bash
   oci network nat-gateway list -c <compartment of that VCN> --query 'data[]."nat-ip"'
   ```

   On a k3s VM with a public IP, it is that IP. The setting applies to clusters created afterwards.
4. Review the default limits and the templates.

Create a small test cluster and watch the Terraform log. It ends with `OK Cluster ready for kubeconfig downloads`; if it reports `Cluster API endpoint … not reachable from Infrayard` instead, fix the API access from step 3. When the cluster reaches **Running**, download the kubeconfig and run `kubectl get nodes`. Destroy the test cluster afterwards. This run proves the OCI policies, the state bucket and the network path to the cluster API; a successful `helm install` alone does not. See [cluster lifecycle](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/cluster-lifecycle/).

### Add users

With the bundled Keycloak, users are managed in the Keycloak admin console, which is not exposed on the internet. Open it through a port forward:

```bash
kubectl port-forward -n infrayard svc/infrayard-keycloak 8080:8080
```

Go to `http://localhost:8080/auth/admin`, sign in as `admin` with the Keycloak master admin password and switch to the realm **infrayard**.

- **Users → Add user**, then **Credentials → Set password** with **Temporary** on.
- For an administrator: **Role mapping → Assign role → admin**.

Users without the `admin` role can sign in, deploy clusters within their limits and see the templates allowed for their roles. To connect Infrayard to your company Keycloak instead, see [Use your own Keycloak](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/).

### Reference: all settings

```bash
helm show values oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard --version <version>
```

Every value is documented in that output. After the installation, `helm status infrayard -n infrayard` prints the portal URL and the sign-in summary again.

Next: [restrict access to your VPN](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/) and plan [upgrades and backups](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/).


## Use your own Keycloak

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/

By default Infrayard brings its own Keycloak with a ready realm. If your company already runs Keycloak, Infrayard can sign users in through a realm there instead, so people use their existing accounts and you manage access with roles or groups you already have.

This option is available for the [Kubernetes installation](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/). It is tested with Keycloak 22 and 26; use Keycloak 22 or newer.

### How sign-in works

1. The portal sends the user to your Keycloak login page (OpenID Connect, Authorization Code flow with PKCE).
2. Keycloak returns an access token to the portal client `infrayard-portal`. It is a public client: there is no client secret to store.
3. The Infrayard API checks the token's signature against the realm keys, its issuer and that it was issued to `infrayard-portal`.
4. On the first sign-in Infrayard creates its own user record from the token. There is no directory sync.

The token must contain `sub`, `preferred_username`, `email` and the roles or groups described below. Keycloak includes them by default.

### Roles

| Role | Default name | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admin role | `admin` | Administration: all clusters, users, configuration, templates, requests and audit log |
| Access role | none | When set, only users with this role (or the admin role) may use Infrayard. Others see "Your account is not allowed to use Infrayard" and are signed out |
| Template roles | your choice, for example `testing`, `production` | Templates can require a role; only users holding it see the template |

In a shared company realm, choose names that cannot clash with existing roles, such as `infrayard-admin` and `infrayard-user`, and always set the access role. Without it, every account in the realm can sign in and create clusters within the default limits.

Infrayard can read these names from one of three places in the token:

| Source | `rolesClaim` value | You assign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Realm roles (default) | `realm_access.roles` | Realm roles, directly or through a group |
| Client roles | `resource_access.infrayard-portal.roles` | Roles of the client `infrayard-portal` |
| Groups | `groups` | Group membership (the group name is compared) |

### 1. Set the Helm values

Add these values to your `values.yaml` from the [Kubernetes guide](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/#4-write-the-values-files):

```yaml
keycloak:
  enabled: false                 # do not install the bundled Keycloak

api:
  oidc:
    issuer: https://sso.example.com/realms/acme
    clientId: infrayard-portal
    rolesClaim: realm_access.roles
    adminRole: infrayard-admin
    requiredRole: infrayard-user
```

The `issuer` must be exactly the `iss` value of your tokens. Check it at `https://sso.example.com/realms/acme/.well-known/openid-configuration`. Keycloak versions before 17, and some installations, use the path `/auth/realms/acme`.

The `keycloak.admin.password` and `keycloak.realmImport` values are not needed in this mode.

### 2. Install and import the client

Install or upgrade with Helm as in the Kubernetes guide. The chart then prepares a Keycloak import file that matches your values: the client, the admin and access roles, and for `rolesClaim: groups` the groups and the group mapper. Export it:

```bash
kubectl get configmap infrayard-oidc-client -n infrayard \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.keycloak-partial-import\.json}' > infrayard-keycloak.json
```

In the Keycloak admin console, open your realm, then **Realm settings → Action (top right) → Partial import**. Select the file, choose **If a resource exists: Skip** and click **Import**.

The imported client `infrayard-portal` is public, uses the Standard flow with PKCE (S256) and allows `https://infrayard.example.com/*` as redirect and post-logout URL.

`helm status infrayard -n infrayard` prints the same instructions with your values.

### 3. Give users access

Assign the admin role and the access role to the right people, preferably through groups. For example, in **Groups → platform-team → Role mapping → Assign role**, add `infrayard-admin`; in **Groups → engineering**, add `infrayard-user`.

Sign in at `https://infrayard.example.com` with an admin account and open **Admin**. A role change takes effect with the user's next token, at the latest after the access token lifetime of your realm (5 minutes by default). Users whose role was removed are signed out with a message; users whose Keycloak session ends are signed out as well.

### Keycloak with a private CA

If Keycloak's certificate comes from an internal company CA, browsers trust it through your device management, but the Infrayard API needs the CA explicitly to fetch the realm keys. Add the CA certificate:

```yaml
api:
  oidc:
    ca:
      cert: |
        -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
        MIIDdzCCAl+gAwIBAgIU...
        -----END CERTIFICATE-----
```

Or reference an existing ConfigMap in the `infrayard` namespace, for example one managed by trust-manager:

```yaml
api:
  oidc:
    ca:
      existingConfigMap: company-ca
      key: ca.crt
```

Public CAs remain trusted in both cases.

### Keycloak under another address inside the cluster

Users reach Keycloak at the public issuer address. If the Infrayard API cannot use that address (split-horizon DNS, no route from the cluster to it), give it an internal address of the same realm:

```yaml
api:
  oidc:
    issuer: https://sso.example.com/realms/acme
    internalUrl: http://keycloak.sso.svc.cluster.local:8080/realms/acme
```

Only the signing keys are fetched there; tokens must still carry the public issuer.

### Changing the role source later

The import uses **Skip** for existing objects. If you later switch to `rolesClaim: groups`, the existing client does not get the group mapper. Add a **Group membership** mapper named `groups` (token claim name `groups`, full group path off) to the client's dedicated scope, or delete the client and import the new file.

### Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| After the Keycloak login the portal does not load your data (API answers 401) | `issuer` differs from the token's `iss` (for example `/auth` in the path). Compare with the realm's `.well-known/openid-configuration` |
| "Your account is not allowed to use Infrayard" | The user lacks the access role, or `rolesClaim` points to the wrong place. Decode a token and check the claim |
| No **Admin** menu for an admin | The admin role is not in the claim named by `rolesClaim` |
| API log: `Cannot fetch OIDC signing keys` | The API cannot reach Keycloak or does not trust its certificate. Set `internalUrl` or `ca` |
| Keycloak error "Invalid parameter: redirect_uri" | The client's redirect URI does not match the Infrayard domain. Re-import, or fix the client's Valid redirect URIs |


## Private access (VPN only)

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/private-access/

Infrayard holds credentials that can create and delete infrastructure in your OCI tenancy. We strongly recommend that the portal is reachable only from your company network or VPN, not from the whole internet. Infrayard does not restrict network access by itself: this is part of your network setup, and this page shows the usual ways to do it.

Keep in mind what still has to work:

- **Inbound:** users on the VPN reach the portal on port 443. With the bundled Keycloak, sign-in runs on the same address under `/auth`, so it becomes private too.
- **Outbound from Infrayard:** OCI APIs, the image registry, and the Kubernetes API (port 6443) of every cluster it creates. A NAT gateway or your proxy path is enough; Infrayard needs no inbound connection from the internet.
- **Clusters:** users need a route from the VPN to the Kubernetes API of their clusters to use `kubectl`. See [Kubernetes API access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/#kubernetes-api-endpoint-access).

### Option A: private address (recommended)

The portal gets an IP address inside your VCN and has no public IP at all. The VPN reaches the VCN through a dynamic routing gateway (Site-to-Site VPN or FastConnect) or through a VPN server in the VCN.

**OKE with Traefik:** install Traefik with an internal load balancer in a private subnet. OCI does not change an existing load balancer from public to private: if Traefik already runs with a public one, remove it first with `helm uninstall traefik -n traefik`. The new load balancer receives a private IP.

```bash
helm install traefik traefik/traefik -n traefik --create-namespace \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-internal"=true \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-subnet1"=<private-subnet-ocid> \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape"=flexible \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-min"=10 \
  --set-string service.annotations."service\.beta\.kubernetes\.io/oci-load-balancer-shape-flex-max"=100
```

Annotations must be strings; with `--set`, Helm reads `true` and the numbers as other types and the install fails.

**Other Kubernetes distributions:** use your platform's internal load balancer, or expose the ingress controller only on the nodes' private addresses.

**k3s on a single VM:** create the VM in a private subnet without a public IP. Give the subnet a NAT gateway for outbound traffic.

### Option B: public address with an allowlist

The portal keeps its public IP, but only your VPN's egress addresses may connect. In OCI, add an ingress rule for TCP 443 (and 80) from your VPN CIDR ranges only, in the network security group or security list of the load balancer or the VM, and remove any rule that allows `0.0.0.0/0`.

This is quicker to set up but depends on the VPN's public addresses staying the same.

### Certificates for a private portal

Let's Encrypt's standard check (HTTP-01) connects to your portal from the internet, so it fails once the portal is private. Choose one of these:

| Certificate | How |
| --- | --- |
| From your company CA | `kubectl create secret tls infrayard-tls -n infrayard --cert=fullchain.pem --key=privkey.pem` and remove the `cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer` annotation from the values |
| Let's Encrypt with a DNS check (DNS-01) | A cert-manager `ClusterIssuer` with a [DNS-01 solver](https://cert-manager.io/docs/configuration/acme/dns01/) for your DNS provider |

A company CA certificate must be trusted on users' devices; for a public DNS-01 certificate nothing extra is needed. Renew company CA certificates before they expire: Infrayard does not do that for you.

### DNS

Point `infrayard.example.com` to the private IP in your internal DNS, for example a private view in OCI DNS or your company DNS that VPN clients use. A public DNS record with a private IP also works, but it publishes the internal address.

### Your own Keycloak

If you [use your own Keycloak](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/), users' browsers must reach it from the VPN, and the Infrayard API must reach it from the cluster. If the API sees Keycloak under a different internal address, set `api.oidc.internalUrl`.

### Cluster API endpoints

Clusters created by Infrayard can use a private Kubernetes API endpoint or a public one restricted to allowed source ranges. With a restricted public endpoint, add the VPN's egress ranges **and** Infrayard's own outbound address to **Allowed API CIDRs** in **Admin → Configuration → OCI Settings**; Infrayard calls the cluster API to issue kubeconfigs. See [networking](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/).

### Check it

From a machine outside the VPN, the portal must not answer:

```bash
curl -m 10 -sS -o /dev/null https://infrayard.example.com && echo "STILL PUBLIC"
```

From the VPN, it must load and sign-in must work. Then create a test cluster and download its kubeconfig to confirm that Infrayard still reaches OCI and the cluster API.


## Cluster lifecycle

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/cluster-lifecycle/

These workflows apply to supported OKE clusters managed through Infrayard. Check your cluster tier and network prerequisites before making changes.

### Signing in

Infrayard signs you in through Keycloak — the bundled instance or your organisation's existing Keycloak. Click **Log In** — you are redirected to the Keycloak login page and returned to the portal after authentication. No separate Infrayard account is needed.

### Deploying a cluster

1. Navigate to **Deploy** from the top nav
2. *(Optional)* Select a **Cluster template** — pre-configured profiles created by your admin that pre-fill and lock resource fields (pools, nodes, CPU, RAM, storage). Choose "Custom" to configure everything manually with your account's limits enforced
3. Enter a **Cluster name** — this becomes the base name for all OCI resources (`{name}-cluster`, `{name}-vcn`, etc.)
4. Choose a **CIDR range** from the available pool — each cluster gets its own /24
5. Select a **Kubernetes version**, **VM shape**, and **Node image** (locked if the template defines them; otherwise user-selectable — image defaults to auto-select if none configured)
6. If using "Custom" mode, configure one or more **Node pools** — each pool has a name, node count, OCPU, RAM, and storage, constrained by your account's effective limits
7. *(Optional)* Use the **Advanced tab** to bring existing OCI infrastructure — your own VCN, compartment, or subnet
8. Review the **Deployment Summary** — shows all resources that will be created, plus live estimated monthly and hourly cost
9. Click **Deploy**

Infrayard runs `terraform apply` and streams the live output in the portal. The cluster appears in **My Clusters** once provisioning completes.

> The deploy form enforces your account's effective limits — maximum pools, nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage. If a limit prevents you from deploying, submit a limit-increase request from the deploy or scale flow; admins can approve granted values into your per-user overrides.

### Scaling a cluster

1. In **My Clusters**, click **Scale** on a running cluster
2. Adjust resources per pool — nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage
3. Add new node pools or remove existing ones as needed; new pools default their name to the cluster's bare name and accept any name that matches the standard pool-name rules (lowercase, alphanumeric + hyphen, 32 chars max). Existing pool names stay immutable to keep Terraform/OKE state aligned.
4. Review the change preview and click **Apply**

Scaling behaviour depends on the cluster tier configured by your admin — see [Cluster tiers](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/cluster-lifecycle/#cluster-tiers).
Kubernetes version changes are handled via a separate **Upgrade** action.

### Destroying a cluster

1. In **My Clusters**, click **Destroy**
2. Infrayard runs `terraform plan -destroy` and shows the exact resources that will be removed
3. Confirm — `terraform destroy` runs and cluster-scoped OCI resources are cleaned up
4. The CIDR range is returned to the pool and available for reuse

Destroy is permanent and cannot be undone.

> **Requests workflow:** The admin **Requests** area handles both protected-cluster destroy approvals and per-user limit-increase requests. Users submit a reason instead of destroying directly or when they need higher limits; admins approve, adjust, or deny with a note. Destroy approval still opens the Terraform destroy plan before force-destroy. Limit approval writes granted values into the user's per-user overrides. Results appear in the user's Activity inbox, and SMTP-enabled installs can also send info-only email pings with requester, action, comments, and request parameters.
>
> **Destroy behavior note:** Infrayard-managed child compartments may be deleted with the cluster. External compartment overrides are retained for shared/multi-cluster setups. In Object Storage, only the destroyed cluster's `.tfstate` object is removed; the user-level prefix/folder is kept for other clusters.

### Activity

The user nav includes an **Activity** inbox with an unread badge. It persists important events across refreshes and sessions; today it records destroy-request approvals/denials, limit request submissions and reviews, TTL expiry warnings at 24h, 4h, and 1h remaining, deploy/scale/upgrade/destroy start and completion events, and admin-driven account limit changes. Administrators also receive the deploy, scale, upgrade and destroy events of other users' clusters, with the owner's name, and an entry for every new destroy or limit request.

### Cluster detail

Click **Details** on any cluster card to see:

- **Cluster information** — name, status, K8s version, region, CIDR, compartment, VM shape, cluster tier, estimated monthly cost, OCID
- **Node pools** — pool name, node count, OCPU, RAM, storage, and status per pool
- **Cost breakdown** — per-pool monthly cost, control plane cost (Enhanced tier), and total with hourly rate
- **Access** — kubeconfig download and SSH key download (see [Kubernetes access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/security/#kubernetes-access))

### Cluster tiers

The admin configures which cluster tier(s) the platform allows: **Basic only**, **Enhanced only**, or **Both**. When a single tier is allowed, users see it as an informational indicator on the deploy form. When **Both** is allowed, the deploy form shows a tier picker so each user picks per cluster — useful when one team wants free/dev clusters and another wants production-grade scaling, all served by the same platform.

| | Basic | Enhanced |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | Free | Oracle's current Enhanced control-plane rate |
| Node scaling | ⚠️ Full — add/remove nodes or pools is automatic; resource-profile changes require manual cycling | ✅ Full in-place |
| Cluster Autoscaler | ❌ | ✅ |
| Best for | Dev/test, cost-sensitive teams | Production, automated scaling |

**Basic cluster scaling:** Both Basic and Enhanced clusters support full scaling — nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage. In Basic clusters, adding/removing nodes or node pools is automatic and does not require manual rotation. Manual cycling is required when changing per-node resources (shape, OCPU, RAM, storage), and is also recommended after a Kubernetes upgrade so workers pick up the new target image/version.

**OKE → Cluster → Node Pool → Nodes → Cordon & drain → Terminate**

Recommended rolling cycle for each affected Basic node pool (current size = `N`):
1. Scale from `N` to `2N`
2. Wait until the additional `N` nodes are `Ready/Active`
3. Scale back from `2N` to `N` (OKE removes extra nodes automatically)
4. Verify workloads and node health before moving to the next pool

The portal shows tier-specific warnings/messages for this flow.

**Kubernetes version upgrades:** Use **Upgrade k8s** on a running cluster. This updates the control plane and node-pool target Kubernetes/image configuration:
- Direct upgrades are limited to the same or next minor version (for example `1.33.x -> 1.34.x`; not `1.33.x -> 1.35.x`).
- Basic: perform rolling worker refresh per pool (`N -> 2N -> N`) after nodes become `Ready/Active`; the Upgrade modal shows live per-pool steps based on current node counts.
- Enhanced: rollout is fully automated (control plane plus worker refresh), no manual cycling required.

**Switching tiers:** Admins can switch the platform tier at any time in Configuration — Basic, Enhanced, or Both. The change applies to all new clusters; existing clusters retain the tier they were provisioned with.

**Per-user tier override:** Admins can pin a specific user to Basic or to Enhanced, regardless of the global setting. The override is force-only (single tier per user); a user without an override inherits whatever the global setting allows, including the per-cluster picker when the global is **Both**.

### Kubernetes upgrades

- **Dedicated action** — available from cluster detail and dashboard actions
- **Shape-aware + allowlist-aware** — upgrade options are filtered to OCI-compatible versions enabled by admin config
- **Sequential minors only** — direct upgrades allow same/next minor only; skip-minor upgrades are blocked with explicit error
- **Control plane + node-pool target update** — upgrade action updates cluster Kubernetes and node-pool target version/image
- **Basic upgrade behavior** — perform rolling worker refresh per pool (`N -> 2N -> N`) after new nodes are `Ready/Active`
- **Enhanced upgrade behavior** — fully automated rollout (control plane + workers), no manual cycling required
- **Tier guidance in UI** — Basic and Enhanced show upgrade-specific notes with rollout guidance
- **Dynamic Basic rollout guidance** — Basic upgrade modal reads live pool/node counts and renders exact per-pool steps (for example `1 -> 2 -> 1` or `3 -> 6 -> 3`) instead of a static example

### Expiry and cleanup

A time-to-live can be set for temporary clusters. When its TTL is reached, Infrayard starts the destroy workflow. Use TTL deliberately and check how it interacts with your protected-cluster policy. Activity includes expiry warnings at 24 hours, 4 hours and 1 hour remaining.

Scaling a Basic cluster to zero worker nodes can pause compute use, but does not guarantee a zero Oracle bill: retained resources and other services can still be charged.

Review [operating responsibilities](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/) before production changes.


## Administration

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/administration/

Administrators configure the approved options and operating boundaries available to each team. Review [security and access](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/security/) for the identity and privilege model.

Admin access is granted by the admin role in Keycloak (`admin` in the bundled realm; with your own Keycloak a realm role, client role or group you choose, see [roles](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/#roles)). Admins see an **Admin** panel in the top navigation.

### All clusters

A full view of every cluster across all users — status, owner, CIDR, K8s version, tier, resource counts, estimated cost (monthly + hourly), and age. The stats cards show online, provisioning, upgrading k8s, destroying, failed, total, CIDRs used, and monthly spend. From this view admins can:

- Click **Details** on any cluster to open its full detail view including kubeconfig and SSH key download
- Click **Scale** on Active/Error clusters to adjust pools, nodes, and per-node resources
- Click **Upgrade k8s** on Active/Error clusters to upgrade Kubernetes version
- Click **Destroy** to destroy any cluster regardless of owner
- Click **View logs** while an operation is running or after a failure
- Click **New Cluster** to provision a cluster outside of normal user quotas

### Users & limits

Lists every user who has signed into Infrayard. For each user, admins can:

- View current cluster count and active limit
- View resolved effective limits (per-user override if set, otherwise global default)
- Click **Edit Limits** to set per-user overrides for any combination of: cluster limit, pool max, node max, OCPU, RAM, storage, and cluster tier
- Reset a user's overrides back to global defaults; direct admin limit edits and resets create user Activity notifications
- Reset all overrides at once to revert the user to global platform defaults

Limit changes take effect on the user's next page load or login — no restart required.

### Configuration

Platform-wide settings manageable at runtime — no redeployment needed:

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| Cluster tier | Basic (free), Enhanced (Oracle's current Enhanced control-plane rate), or Both — applies to all new clusters; "Both" lets the user pick per cluster on the deploy form |
| Cluster limit | Default max active clusters per user |
| Node pool limit | Max pools per cluster |
| Nodes per pool | Max nodes per pool |
| OCPU / RAM / Storage | Max compute per node |
| CIDR pool | Add, remove, and enable/disable /24 ranges available for cluster allocation |
| VM shapes | Sync from OCI, plus add/remove/enable/disable shapes in the deploy form |
| K8s versions | Add, remove, and enable/disable Kubernetes versions |
| Node images | Add, remove, and enable/disable OCI compute images for worker node pools |
