> Note: Shape and image availability is region- and tenancy-specific. In **Admin → Configuration**, use **Sync from OCI** in the VM Shapes section first, then curate/label as needed. For CLI verification, fetch current OKE node pool options in the target region:
>
> `oci ce node-pool-options get --node-pool-option-id all --profile <PROFILE>`
>
> Use the returned `shapes` and `sources` lists as the source of truth for VM shapes and node images.
>
> If **Sync from OCI** is unavailable, Infrayard keeps existing shape config unchanged and you can continue with manual curation from the CLI output above. Sync uses the API pod OCI service account credentials/policies (not the browser/user profile).
>
> K8s version freshness: OCI can publish new OKE patch versions after Infrayard is deployed. The platform now auto-syncs available OKE versions in the background (default daily) so admin config stays current without anyone clicking **Refresh from OCI**. Newly-fetched versions land disabled by default — admins still curate which versions users may deploy. **Refresh from OCI** remains available for on-demand pulls (e.g. before template reviews or upgrade waves). Upgrade recommendation pills use the latest enabled version, so stale enablement can hide available upgrades.
>
> Once a cluster's K8s version falls behind the latest enabled, a separate sweeper (default hourly) emits one Activity entry plus one email to the cluster owner per (cluster, target version) pair, so the owner is told about new upgrade options even when not actively logged in. The notification is idempotent — it does not re-fire for the same target — and the marker auto-resets after the cluster is upgraded, ready to fire again on the next enabled-version bump.
>
> Deploy form behavior: Kubernetes versions are filtered by the currently selected VM shape and region. Users only see versions that are both OCI-compatible for that shape (based on OKE node image availability) and enabled in Admin Configuration. If compatibility lookup is unavailable, the K8s list is not shown (fail-closed) and deploy is blocked until validation succeeds. If a version is missing, either enable it in Admin Configuration or choose a shape that supports it.

### Cluster templates

Templates are administrator-approved configurations. Template-defined resource values can exceed a user's personal custom-deployment limits; the locked fields prevent the user from editing those pre-approved values. Review template scope and required roles accordingly.

Dedicated admin page for creating and managing cluster templates — pre-configured profiles that appear as selectable cards on the deploy form. Templates encode:

| Setting | Description |
|---|---|
| K8s version | Pre-selected Kubernetes version (optional — user selects if not set) |
| VM shape | Pre-selected node shape (optional) |
| Node image | Pre-selected OCI compute image (optional — auto-selects latest OKE image if not set) |
| Node pools | Pre-defined pool layout — name, node count, OCPU, RAM, storage per pool |
| Tier default | Suggested cluster tier — Basic or Enhanced (suggestion only, not enforced) |
| TTL | Optional time-to-live in hours — when reached, Infrayard automatically starts cluster destroy/cleanup |
| Destroy protection | When enabled, the "Destroy" button on the user's cluster opens a "Request destroy" modal instead. Requests land in Admin → Requests (with a live count badge in the nav) where an admin approves, reviews the destroy plan, then confirms force-destroy, or denies with a note |
| Required role | Keycloak role (or group, depending on your role source) — only users with it can see and use the template. Leave empty for all users |
| Sort order | Controls display position in the deploy form (lower numbers appear first) |

The templates table shows estimated monthly and hourly cost per template. The add/edit modal includes a live cost preview that updates as you change pools, shape, or tier.

Template modal behavior: when a VM shape is selected, the K8s dropdown is filtered to versions OCI reports as compatible for that shape in the current region (node-image-backed compatibility). If compatibility lookup is unavailable, no fallback list is shown (fail-closed). Template save/update re-validates shape+K8s compatibility and blocks incompatible combinations.

**Environment-tier gating** — use `required_role` to control which teams can deploy which cluster sizes. For example, create a `DEV — Small` template visible to everyone, a `TEST — Medium` template requiring a `testing` role, a `UAT — Large` template requiring a `uat` role, and a `PROD — HA` template requiring a `production` role. Users only see the templates they have access to on the deploy form. Create the roles in Keycloak under **Realm roles** (or as client roles or groups, matching your [role source](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/#roles)) and assign them to the relevant users.

Templates can be created, edited, enabled/disabled, and permanently deleted. Disabled templates no longer appear in the deploy form but remain referenced by existing clusters. Permanently deleting a template removes it from the admin panel entirely.

### Requests

Approval queue for user-submitted destroy requests on protection-enabled clusters and limit-increase requests for per-user overrides. The admin nav shows live request count badges that refresh every 5 seconds (hidden when zero pending). Filter by Pending / Approved / Denied / All. Each pending row has a **Review** action. When SMTP is configured, request submit/review events also send info-only email pings: admins get submit notifications, and users get submit/approve/deny notifications.

For destroy requests, the review modal lets the admin:
- Add an optional admin note
- Click **Approve & review plan** — the normal destroy plan opens. After the admin confirms the plan, the request is marked `approved` and `force=true` destroy starts. Audit-logged as `destroy-request:approve`.
- Click **Deny** — the note is surfaced on the user's cluster card as a red "Destroy denied" pill (with the note in the tooltip). Audit-logged as `destroy-request:deny`.

For limit requests, the review modal lets the admin grant the requested values or adjust them before approval. Approved values are written into the user's per-user overrides and the user receives an Activity notification. Denials can include an admin note and are audit-logged as `limit-request:deny`. Request emails include the requester, request id, comment, requested values, and granted values where applicable.

Approval is row-locked to prevent two admins double-approving. Bypass path: admins can still force-destroy any protected cluster directly via `?force=true` from the All Clusters table — useful for incident response.

### Audit Log

Every provisioning, scaling, upgrade, and destroy operation is recorded with user identity, operation type, cluster name, outcome, and duration — including `destroy-request:*` and `limit-request:*` events from the Requests queue. The log is append-only and filterable by user, operation, and date range.

### Resource limits

Limits cascade: global config sets the baseline for all users, per-user overrides take precedence when set.

| Limit | Global default | Per-user override |
|---|---|---|
| Clusters per user | Inherited from config | ✅ |
| Node pools per cluster | 3 | ✅ |
| Nodes per pool | 3 | ✅ |
| OCPU per node | 1 | ✅ |
| RAM per node | 12 GB | ✅ |
| Storage per node | 50 GB | ✅ |
| Cluster tier | BASIC_CLUSTER | ✅ |

The deploy form always reflects the user's current effective limits. If a user hits a limit, the form shows a clear message with a link to contact support. Limits can be raised at any time by an admin without restarting the platform.

### Cost estimates

Cost estimates are visible in deployment forms, cluster cards, cluster details, templates and administrator views. They use configured resource rates with optional overrides for custom contracts. The breakdown covers the modelled compute, worker storage and control-plane components; it is not a reconciliation of your Oracle invoice.

Review the rates and included components against your contract. Networking, load balancers, other services and the platform host can add charges outside the cluster estimate. Administrators can review estimated spend across active clusters. Estimates do not enforce a guaranteed monetary budget and do not include the Infrayard subscription.


## Operations, upgrades and recovery

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/

You operate the Infrayard installation; Solvia Lab supplies releases, documentation and support. This page covers upgrades, backups, restores and uninstalling, with the commands to run. They are the same on OKE and k3s.

### Responsibilities

| Area | Who |
| --- | --- |
| Host (Kubernetes cluster or k3s VM), ingress, TLS, storage, network | You |
| OCI user, policies and keys | You |
| Backups of the database, secrets and Terraform state | You |
| Applications on the OKE clusters | You |
| Infrayard releases, release notes, documentation, support | Solvia Lab |

### What to back up

| Item | Contains | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PostgreSQL database `infrayard` | Clusters, jobs, users, configuration, templates, requests, audit log, SSH keys of the worker nodes and, with the bundled Keycloak, all Keycloak users and settings | [Database backup](#backups), daily |
| Terraform state bucket | The state of every managed cluster | Object versioning on the bucket; optionally a copy to another region |
| Configuration | `values.yaml` and `secrets.yaml` | Your secret manager (`secrets.yaml`) and configuration repository (`values.yaml`) |
| OCI API key | `oci_api_key.pem` | Your secret manager |

Database and state belong together: a restored database must match the clusters that actually exist in OCI. Treat backups as sensitive; they contain SSH private keys and, with the bundled Keycloak, password hashes.

### Backups

The database backup is one file that contains both Infrayard and the bundled Keycloak.

```bash
kubectl exec -n infrayard infrayard-postgresql-0 -c postgresql -- \
  pg_dump -U infrayard -Fc infrayard > infrayard-$(date +%F).dump
```

Copy the files off the host, for example to an Object Storage bucket with `oci os object put`, and delete old ones according to your retention policy.

If you use an external PostgreSQL (`postgresql.enabled: false`), back it up with your database tooling instead.

### Restore

Restore into the same Infrayard version that created the backup, then upgrade if needed. Stop the services that write to the database first.

```bash
kubectl scale deploy -n infrayard infrayard-api infrayard-keycloak --replicas=0
kubectl exec -i -n infrayard infrayard-postgresql-0 -c postgresql -- \
  pg_restore -U infrayard -d infrayard --clean --if-exists --no-owner < infrayard-2026-01-31.dump
kubectl scale deploy -n infrayard infrayard-api infrayard-keycloak --replicas=1
```

Without the bundled Keycloak, leave `infrayard-keycloak` out of the commands.

**On a new host**, start only the database first, so that nothing writes to it before the restore: install with your values and `--set api.replicaCount=0 --set keycloak.replicaCount=0`, restore, then run `helm upgrade` with the same command without these two options.

After a restore, compare the cluster list in the portal with what exists in OCI before you start new operations. A cluster created or destroyed after the backup appears in the wrong state; its Terraform state in the bucket is still correct.

### Upgrade Infrayard

Before you start:

1. Read the release notes of the target version, especially for steps marked as required.
2. Take a [database backup](#backups).
3. Make sure no cluster operation is running (**Admin → All Clusters**).

The API applies database changes automatically when it starts. They cannot be undone by downgrading; a rollback means restoring the backup.

```bash
helm upgrade infrayard oci://registry.gitlab.com/solvialab/infrayard/charts/infrayard \
  --version 1.5.0 -n infrayard -f values.yaml -f secrets.yaml
kubectl get pods -n infrayard -w
```

The chart version selects the image version. Changed configuration or secrets restart the affected pods automatically.

**After the upgrade:** sign in as an administrator and as a regular user, check the cluster list and the Activity history, and run **Sync** in **Admin → Configuration** to confirm OCI access.

**Rollback:** `helm rollback infrayard -n infrayard` returns the previous chart and images. If the new version had already started, also restore the backup taken before the upgrade.

### PostgreSQL and Keycloak versions

The chart pins the PostgreSQL major version (currently 18) and the Keycloak version (currently 26.8). Patch releases arrive with Infrayard upgrades.

A new PostgreSQL major version cannot read the old data directory. When a release moves to a new major version, its notes say so, and the upgrade needs a dump and restore:

1. Take a [database backup](#backups).
2. Stop everything and delete the database volume: `kubectl scale deploy -n infrayard infrayard-api infrayard-keycloak --replicas=0`, then `kubectl delete statefulset infrayard-postgresql -n infrayard` and `kubectl delete pvc data-infrayard-postgresql-0 -n infrayard`.
3. Start the new version with only the database running: the `helm upgrade` command from above with `--set api.replicaCount=0 --set keycloak.replicaCount=0`.
4. [Restore](#restore) the backup with the `pg_restore` command.
5. Start everything: the same `helm upgrade` without the two `--set` options.

Keycloak updates its schema by itself on the first start of a new version.

### OKE clusters are a separate topic

Upgrading Infrayard does not touch your OKE clusters. Kubernetes upgrades of the clusters are done per cluster in the portal; see [cluster lifecycle](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/cluster-lifecycle/). Plan them with worker refresh, disruption budgets and temporary extra capacity in mind.

### Uninstall Infrayard

Uninstalling Infrayard does not touch the clusters it created, and only Infrayard can destroy them cleanly: their Terraform state is in the state bucket. Work through the steps in this order.

1. **Destroy the clusters** you no longer need in the portal and wait until each one is destroyed. A destroyed cluster takes its compartment, VCN and node pools with it. Clusters you keep go on running and being billed.
2. **Back up the database** if you may need the history later; see [backups](#backups).
3. **Remove Infrayard.** Helm keeps the PostgreSQL volume; deleting the claim deletes the volume as well, on OKE the 50 GB `oci-bv` block volume. The namespace also holds the registry and OCI key secrets:

   ```bash
   helm uninstall infrayard -n infrayard
   kubectl delete pvc -n infrayard data-infrayard-postgresql-0
   kubectl delete namespace infrayard
   ```

4. **Remove Traefik and cert-manager** if you installed them only for Infrayard in step 1 of the [Kubernetes guide](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/). When Traefik is removed, OKE deletes its load balancer. cert-manager leaves its CRDs behind; the last command deletes them:

   ```bash
   helm uninstall traefik -n traefik
   helm uninstall cert-manager -n cert-manager
   kubectl delete clusterissuer letsencrypt
   kubectl delete namespace traefik cert-manager
   kubectl get crd -o name | grep 'cert-manager.io$' | xargs kubectl delete
   ```

5. **Check OCI.** On OKE, after a minute or two the load balancer is gone and the block volume is `TERMINATED` in the compartment of the cluster that ran Infrayard:

   ```bash
   oci lb load-balancer list -c <compartment>
   oci bv volume list -c <compartment> --query 'data[].{name:"display-name",state:"lifecycle-state"}'
   ```

6. **Delete the state bucket** once none of its clusters is left. Versioning is on, so `--empty` removes every object version before the bucket:

   ```bash
   oci os bucket delete --bucket-name infrayard-tfstate --empty --force
   ```

7. **Remove the rest by hand** if no other installation uses it: the DNS record of the portal, and the OCI user, group and policy from [OCI setup](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/).

If you destroy the cluster that runs Infrayard, remove the load balancer and the volume first (steps 3 to 5). OKE does not delete them with the cluster: the load balancer keeps the VCN from being deleted, and the volume stays and is billed.

### Ending a subscription

Ending the subscription does not stop or delete anything in OCI, and Oracle keeps billing running clusters. Before access ends, destroy the clusters you no longer need, or keep the Terraform state bucket so that they can still be managed. Details are in your agreement; see [billing and licensing](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/subscription/#cancellation-and-offboarding).


## Troubleshooting and support

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/troubleshooting/

Start with the logs. For a failed cluster operation, open the operation's Terraform log in the portal. For the installation itself:

```bash
# Kubernetes
kubectl get pods -n infrayard
kubectl describe pod -n infrayard <pod>
kubectl logs -n infrayard deploy/infrayard-api --tail=200
```

Note the time and the exact error before you retry, and check what actually exists in OCI before starting a second operation on the same cluster.

### Installation

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| `infrayard-api` pod stays in `Init` or `ContainerCreating`; events mention `infrayard-oci-key` | The OCI key secret is missing or in another namespace. Create it as in [step 3](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/#3-create-the-namespace-and-secrets) |
| `ImagePullBackOff`, or `helm show chart` fails with `401`, `403`, `unauthorized` or `denied` | The registry login or the `regcred` secret is missing, has a typo, or the token has expired. Check `global.imagePullSecrets` and the image addresses. If the login succeeds but pulling still fails, the token lacks read access to the registry; ask support for a new token |
| API log or `oci` CLI shows `401 NotAuthenticated` right after the OCI user or API key was created | OCI needs a few minutes to activate a new user and key in every service. Wait five minutes and retry. If it persists, compare the fingerprint, user OCID and tenancy OCID with the API key page |
| API log shows `404 NotAuthorizedOrNotFound` for OCI calls | A policy statement is missing or names the wrong group or compartment. Compare with [Prepare OCI](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/oci-setup/#3-add-the-policies) |
| Traefik install on OKE fails with `cannot unmarshal number into Go struct field ObjectMeta.metadata.annotations of type string` | The load balancer annotations were passed with `--set`, which turns `10` and `100` into numbers. Use `--set-string` as in [step 1](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/#1-ingress-controller-and-certificates) |
| Pod stays in `Init:ImageInspectError`; events show `short name mode is enforcing` | OKE nodes run CRI-O, which accepts only fully qualified image names. An image override such as `postgres:18-alpine` must name its registry: `docker.io/library/postgres:18-alpine` |
| After a `helm upgrade` that fixes an image or setting, `infrayard-postgresql-0` keeps its old error | A StatefulSet does not replace a pod that never became ready. Delete it with `kubectl delete pod -n infrayard infrayard-postgresql-0`; it starts again with the new settings and keeps its volume |
| `helm install` fails with `... is required` | A required value is missing, for example `postgresql.auth.password` or `keycloak.admin.password`. Add it to `secrets.yaml` |
| Certificate stays `READY False` | DNS does not point to the ingress yet, or port 80 is not reachable from the internet. Check `kubectl describe certificate -n infrayard infrayard-tls` and `kubectl get challenges -A` |
| Sign-in shows `502 Bad Gateway` or a Keycloak error page | Keycloak is still starting (about a minute on the first start) or the realm import failed. Check the Keycloak logs for `Realm 'infrayard' imported` |
| Keycloak does not start, log shows `password authentication failed` | The database password changed after the first start. The database keeps the password it was created with; set the original value again |

### Sign-in and roles

| Symptom | Cause and fix |
| --- | --- |
| "Your account is not allowed to use Infrayard" | The user lacks the access role (`requiredRole`). Assign it in Keycloak; it takes effect at the next sign-in |
| No **Admin** menu | The user lacks the admin role, or `rolesClaim` points to the wrong claim |
| Sign-in works but data does not load | The issuer setting does not match the token. See [Keycloak troubleshooting](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/keycloak/#troubleshooting) |
| A template is missing for a user | The template requires a role the user does not hold |
| A role change has no effect | Roles are read from the token; the user gets the change with the next token, within the token lifetime (5 minutes by default) |

### Missing versions or shapes

In **Admin → Configuration**, sync shapes and Kubernetes versions from OCI for the configured region. Newly found Kubernetes versions must be enabled by an administrator. A version is only offered when OCI has a node image for it and the selected shape.

If the check with OCI fails, deployment is blocked on purpose. Then check the OCI user's policies and the API's outbound access. With the OCI CLI configured for the same user, this shows what OCI offers:

```bash
oci ce node-pool-options get --node-pool-option-id all --region eu-frankfurt-1
```

### Existing-network validation fails

- An existing subnet also needs its VCN OCID.
- The compartment must be the anchor or below it.
- A compartment alone does not reuse its VCN; Infrayard creates a new one.
- With **Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist** on, existing VCNs and subnets are rejected.

See [networking](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/networking/#bringing-your-own-network).

### Worker nodes do not become ready

Look at the Terraform log and the node pool in the OCI Console. Common causes: service limits or quotas, no capacity for the shape in the availability domain, or a shape without a matching image. With your own subnet, the subnet needs a NAT gateway route and a service gateway route; without them nodes cannot register.

### kubectl cannot connect

The kubeconfig only authenticates; it does not open a network path. Check that you are on the VPN, that the cluster's endpoint mode fits your network, and that your egress range is in **Allowed API CIDRs** (**Admin → Configuration → OCI Settings**). Infrayard's own outbound address must be in the allowlist as well, otherwise the kubeconfig download fails; the deploy log then ends with `Cluster API endpoint … not reachable from Infrayard`. See [step 7 of the Kubernetes guide](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/install-kubernetes/#7-sign-in) for how to find that address.

### A limit blocks a request

Check the global default, the user's own limit and the template. Users can request more in the portal; administrators approve or adjust it in **Requests**. Templates may allow more than a user's limit for custom configurations.

### A cluster operation fails

Read the Terraform log, then check the resources in OCI. A failed deployment offers a cleanup action that removes partial resources; check what it will remove first. For Basic clusters, changes to nodes or a Kubernetes upgrade need a rolling worker refresh.

Do not repair Infrayard-managed resources by hand in the OCI Console as a routine fix; the next Terraform run overwrites the changes. If you must intervene, contact support before running further operations on that cluster.

### Contact support

Write to [support@infrayard.eu](mailto:support@infrayard.eu) or use the [support form](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=support#demo). Include:

- The Infrayard version and where it runs (OKE, k3s or other Kubernetes).
- What you did, the approximate time and the region.
- The error message and the relevant log lines.
- Recent changes and what you have already tried.

Remove private keys, tokens, passwords and personal data before you send logs. Response times and support hours are part of your subscription; see [Enterprise](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=enterprise#demo) for extended support.


## Subscription, billing and licensing

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/subscription/

Infrayard is commercial software deployed into the customer environment. Business can be purchased monthly or annually. Subscriptions and registry access are arranged directly with Solvia Lab through a commercial order and onboarding.

### Business pricing

| Billing option | Price | Commitment and payment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monthly | €3,000 per month | One billing month, paid in advance |
| Annual | €30,000 per year | Twelve months, paid upfront; equivalent to €2,500 per month |

Annual payment saves €6,000 compared with twelve monthly payments. Oracle Cloud usage is billed separately by Oracle. Any applicable taxes and the contracted deployment scope are specified in your quote or invoice.

### What you receive

When the order is accepted and the first invoice is paid, your technical contact receives the onboarding e-mail: the registry user and token, the chart and image addresses, the version to install and the support address. [Installation](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/installation/#what-you-receive) lists its contents. With it, your team installs Infrayard on its own with the public guides; they plan about an hour, including the OCI preparation.

| | Business | Enterprise | Guided evaluation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Use | One production and one test installation | Agreed in the proposal | Non-production, 30 days |
| Registry access to the Helm chart and images | For the subscription term | For the agreed term | For the evaluation period |
| New releases | Included | Included | Included during the evaluation |
| Product features | All available features | All available features | All available features |
| Installation | By your team with the public guides | Deployment and rollout assistance as agreed | A guided deployment session |
| Onboarding | Onboarding workshop | As agreed | Agreed scope and success criteria |
| Support | E-mail, 48-hour response in business hours | Agreed response times and escalation | E-mail in business hours |

### What your subscription covers

Business includes the commercial production subscription for one production installation and one non-production test installation, released images and deployment assets, core OKE lifecycle workflows, templates, role-based access, resource limits, protected requests, cost estimates, execution logs and activity history. It includes an onboarding workshop and email support.

Business support has a 48-hour response SLA during the business hours defined in the agreement. Response is not a guaranteed incident resolution time. Your order identifies the covered installations and tenancy, support calendar and authorised contacts. More installations or tenancies are arranged through Enterprise; this website does not imply unlimited installations, tenancies or managed-service resale.

The customer operates the installation, OCI resources and workloads unless additional assistance is agreed. See [operations and responsibilities](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/).

### Founding customer offer

The first 5 qualifying customers receive 40% off Business for their first 12 months.

| Billing option | Founding price | First-year comparison |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monthly | €1,800 per month | Twelve payments total €21,600 |
| Annual | €18,000 for twelve months, paid upfront | Equivalent to €1,500 per month |

The founding period begins when the production subscription starts. Monthly billing keeps the monthly cancellation option; it does not create a twelve-month minimum. The discount ends after the first twelve months and does not restart after cancellation or a billing change. Qualification and availability are confirmed in the order.

The order states the standard renewal price in advance. Current standard Business rates are €3,000 monthly or €30,000 annually; any later change must follow the terms and notice in that agreement. Founding access is to the available Business product. Feedback sessions are available directly with the founder. Public case studies require a separate agreement. Planned features are not guaranteed by participation.

### Enterprise

Enterprise starts from €6,500 per month. The proposal defines billing cadence, commitment, covered scope, deployment assistance, response times, escalation arrangements and any procurement or delivery requirements.

A price shown per month does not establish an Enterprise cancellation right or a particular SLA. Those conditions are agreed in the proposal. [Discuss your requirements](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=enterprise#demo).

### Evaluation

A paid evaluation is optional. After a demo and prerequisite review, a customer can start a monthly production subscription directly.

The optional guided evaluation costs €1,500 for 30 days in your own tenancy, for non-production validation. Agree scope, success criteria and environment readiness first. The window starts when the agreed prerequisites are ready and the evaluation is activated.

The evaluation includes a guided deployment session, time-limited registry access, the same public installation guides and business-hours email support. A single VM with k3s in your tenancy is enough; see [installation](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/installation/). Oracle usage remains payable to Oracle. Evaluation access ends with the agreed evaluation period; production use requires a production subscription.

The full evaluation fee is credited once against your first production invoice if the production order is accepted within 30 days after the evaluation ends. This applies to monthly or annual Business, qualifying Founding Business or an agreed Enterprise order. The fee is not described as a refundable deposit. [Discuss an evaluation](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=evaluation#demo).

### Change from monthly to annual

You can request an annual term after starting monthly. Agree the transition date and credit for any unused, already paid subscription time before the annual invoice is issued. The annual term then runs for twelve months from the agreed start date. A billing change does not restart the founding discount period; any founding-period transition is documented in the revised order.

### Cancellation and offboarding

Monthly Business can be cancelled before the next renewal by contacting [hello@infrayard.eu](mailto:hello@infrayard.eu). It ends at the close of the current paid billing period. Annual subscriptions cover the full paid twelve-month term. Refunds, Enterprise commitments and any exceptional termination rights follow the signed commercial terms.

Agree offboarding before access ends, including required configuration, operational records, Terraform state and supported credential handover. Production licence rights, updates, registry access and support follow the entitlement period and the agreement. Do not assume that cancelling the software subscription deletes or stops OCI resources; Oracle usage charges continue for resources left running.

### Licence and delivery

The commercial agreement governs production rights, deployment scope and restrictions. Standard delivery includes released images, registry access, the Helm chart and documentation. Product source code and release automation are not included unless separately agreed. Managed-service resale and redistribution require explicit written permission.

This public website and documentation do not grant an open-source or Business Source License to the commercial product and do not change rights granted under any separately issued licence. See the [website legal notice](https://www.infrayard.eu/legal/terms.html) and your commercial agreement.

### Start a subscription

[Request a demo](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=demo#demo) or contact [hello@infrayard.eu](mailto:hello@infrayard.eu). We confirm product fit, deployment scope and terms before arranging access. The public website does not collect a card payment or automatically provision a subscription.


## Releases and roadmap

Canonical page: https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/releases/

Choose Infrayard based on capabilities available in the release delivered to your organisation. Planned work is described separately below and is not a delivery commitment unless included in a written agreement.

### Available capabilities

- Create, scale, upgrade, access and destroy OKE clusters through the portal.
- Inspect Terraform execution logs and lifecycle status.
- Publish cluster templates and control role visibility.
- Configure global limits, per-user overrides and limit-increase requests.
- Protect cluster destruction with an admin review workflow.
- Use supported existing OCI compartments, VCNs and subnets.
- Download Kubernetes access files without requiring local OCI CLI setup in the default access workflow.
- Review cost estimates, Activity notifications and audit history.
- Sync available shapes and Kubernetes versions with compatibility filtering.
- Sign in through the bundled Keycloak or your existing Keycloak.
- Install with Helm on Kubernetes: OKE, k3s and other distributions.

Operational behaviour depends on cluster tier and network design; see [requirements](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/requirements/) and [cluster lifecycle](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/cluster-lifecycle/).

### Versioned delivery

Each release has a version number such as `1.4.0`. The Helm chart and the images of a release share that version and are published together in the private registry you receive access to; chart `1.4.0` runs images `1.4.0`.

Each release is announced by e-mail to your technical contact, with release notes that list the changes and any required upgrade steps. Follow [Upgrade Infrayard](https://www.infrayard.eu/docs/operations/#upgrade-infrayard) and run `helm list -n infrayard` to see which version you run. Source code and build pipelines are not needed to install or operate Infrayard.

### Planned work

| Area | Direction |
| --- | --- |
| Gatekeeper AI | Optional assistance for cluster requests and Terraform failures, plus cost and policy insights; customer-controlled provider configuration |
| Cost and policy insights | Idle-cluster signals, anomaly alerts, right-sizing suggestions, drift and lifecycle risk visibility |
| Oracle database options | Optional Oracle-native database deployment backend alongside the existing PostgreSQL approach |
| In-cluster access agent | A future connectivity option for environments that cannot expose even a CIDR-restricted OKE API endpoint |
| Multicloud governance | Read-only inventory and governance for observed EKS, AKS and GKE clusters before lifecycle ownership |
| Non-OCI provisioning | Provider-specific lifecycle automation selected according to customer demand |
| OCI Marketplace | A future listing and guided deployment path |

These items can change in scope and order. Observing an external cluster does not imply Terraform state import or resource adoption. AI, multicloud and Marketplace capabilities are not included as available features solely because they appear here.

### Request release information

For the current supported release, compatibility notes or upgrade guidance for your installation, contact [support@infrayard.eu](mailto:support@infrayard.eu). For product fit and upcoming requirements, [request a demo](https://www.infrayard.eu/?enquiry=demo#demo).
